messages.content: Write a page comparing a managed database service with running your own, for a technical audience choosing between them. Around 250 words.

# Managed database or self-hosted: how to choose

A managed service — RDS, Cloud SQL, Atlas, PlanetScale — takes patching, backups, failover, and version upgrades off your plate. You get a dashboard, an SLA, and a bill that grows with usage. Below a few hundred thousand dollars in infrastructure spend, this usually wins: engineering hours cost more than the markup.

Running your own database, on bare metal or self-managed VMs, buys back three things: cost at scale, control over configuration, and freedom from vendor lock-in. A team running Postgres on its own hardware can tune kernel parameters, pick unusual storage layouts, or run a fork no managed provider offers. At high volume, the gap between a managed service's per-GB pricing and raw disk cost adds up fast — Basecamp and 37signals have written publicly about six- and seven-figure annual savings after leaving the cloud.

The catch is staffing. Self-hosting needs someone on call who understands replication topology, backup verification, and disk failure recovery — not occasionally, but as a standing job. Skip that investment and a self-hosted database turns into a liability: backups nobody tested, a failover nobody rehearsed.

A reasonable default: start managed. Move to self-hosted once cost or control requirements are proven, not projected, and only with a team that treats operations as a real discipline. Making that switch once, on purpose, beats reversing it after a bad month.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

# Managed database or self-hosted: how to choose

A managed service — RDS, Cloud SQL, Atlas, PlanetScale — takes patching, backups, failover, and version upgrades off your plate. You get a dashboard, an SLA, and a bill that scales with usage. Below a few hundred thousand dollars a year in infrastructure spend, this is the right call: engineering time costs more than the markup.

Self-hosting, on bare metal or your own VMs, buys back three things: cost at scale, control over configuration, and freedom from vendor lock-in. A team running its own Postgres can tune kernel parameters, choose an unusual storage layout, or run a fork no managed provider offers. At high volume, the gap between a managed service's per-GB pricing and raw disk cost adds up — Basecamp has written publicly about six- and seven-figure annual savings after moving off the cloud.

The catch is staffing. Self-hosting needs someone on call who understands replication topology, backup verification, and disk failure recovery — not occasionally, but as a standing job. Skip that investment and a self-hosted database becomes a liability: backups nobody has tested, a failover nobody has rehearsed.

A reasonable default: start managed. Move to self-hosted once cost or control requirements are proven, not projected, and only with a team that treats operations as a real discipline. Make that switch once, deliberately — reversing it after a bad month costs far more.
